item.title: Share Your Starlink Internet With the Community and Earn Income
item.content:encoded:
It's also unclear whether the program will be available in all regions. Also, there are no details on pass prices or what the host's payout would look like.

Reselling services on a Residential or Roam plan violates Starlink's Terms of Service. Starlink has been known to suspend service for accounts if it detects higher-than-normal data usage, determines the user may be using it for business purposes, and urges them to switch to a Priority/Enterprise plan to resume service. 

The community site plan may be a compromise for users who don't want a full business plan but want to distribute access to a modest number of people in their community. Plus, it's another revenue source for Starlink. It's also a way for the company to combat the secondary market for its service, such as owners who rent out their Starlink kits for a profit, another violation of its Terms.  

Depending on the scope of usage you describe in your sign-up form, Starlink may recommend a business plan. The program seems geared toward spaces like community centers, public spaces, rural businesses, single buildings with multiple residences, or multiple households in close proximity. 

An ideal use case could be low-income areas without reliable internet access, where the host's Starlink income contributes to subscription costs and other community needs. It's still hard to tell, since it's unclear what the host's share of the pass revenue will be.

item.title: Starship Kicks-Off Next-Generation Starlink
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX has taken a major step toward its many ambitions, including delivering gigabit satellite internet and becoming a dominant broadband provider worldwide. SpaceX launched its 14th Starship flight on September 28, successfully deploying 24 next-generation Starlink satellites that the company claims will greatly improve satellite internet performance.

The fully reusable Starship vehicle is central to Starlink's future roadmap. Engineered for mass deployment and rapid reusability, Starship is the only launch vehicle capable of carrying the heavier payloads required for Starlink's third-generation constellation upgrades.

Supported by the “Mechazilla” launch tower, which is designed to catch the returning booster, SpaceX aims to achieve a cadence where Starship can launch, land, refuel, and fly again within hours. According to SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell, the company envisions flying Starship up to 400 times over the next four years.

item.title: The 10 Small Towns with the Fastest and Slowest Rural Internet 2026
item.content:encoded:
Early 2026 saw several changes across the country that have helped more communities access broadband, whether through fiber or newer alternatives like 5G wireless and low-Earth orbit satellite internet. 

Most importantly, the $42 billion federal Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program is currently funding new physical fiber networks in unserved areas. Since its creation in 2021, it has faced several roadblocks to its goal of bridging the digital divide in the country's most underserved areas. Now states and municipalities are finally getting approval for funding to roll out new broadband initiatives specifically for rural communities.

Technology innovations have also played a role. While fiber-to-the-home networks are more expensive and slower to build out, wireless 5G has emerged as a major competitor. Familiar mobile networks like T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T have each launched home internet service that can compete with traditional wired internet without major infrastructure construction, bringing broadband speeds to the country's most remote areas.

Going even further, LEO satellite internet technology has emerged, led by SpaceX's Starlink. This differs from legacy satellite internet, which uses geostationary orbit satellites that, while effective, can't deliver internet speeds and latency that match terrestrial internet. LEO satellites represent a huge jump in performance, and unlike most terrestrial providers, Starlink isn't limited in availability and can be used nearly anywhere in the U.S. as long as the sky is clear. 

While Starlink is still a newer internet solution, its worldwide customer base has grown exponentially, with the company claiming 12 million total customers in mid-2026. Speeds and availability of LEO satellite internet are expected to keep climbing into 2027 with the upcoming launch of Amazon Leo internet service and the rollout of Starlink's next-generation satellite constellation, which is expected to deliver gigabit speeds when complete.

Better internet may be closer in reach than you think. A helpful way to see which providers are available is to use the FCC's National Broadband Map. It's frequently updated to show which providers are available at your address, so you may have more options than when you first shopped around.

If you're wondering whether fiber is being planned for your area in the near future, contact your local utility companies. Electric utility providers have played a big role in building out fiber because their existing infrastructure and rights-of-way make it easier to reach rural households. Your local utility may have partnered with independent providers, or may even be leading the effort to expand fiber availability. It can't hurt to find out if you could be one of the first in town.

Despite the superiority of a fiber connection, many places still can't make it work because it's too impractical or lacks the investment to become reality. Luckily, 5G wireless and satellite are filling in the gap. Legacy satellite and fixed-wireless providers have made rural internet possible for years, but technology has taken an extraordinary leap forward, and broadband speeds are now possible. Switching to 5G wireless supported by national networks can boost speeds, while Starlink satellite internet continues to improve performance and network capacity.

item.title: Starlink Quietly Expands Free Mini Rentals Beyond the Max Plan
item.content:encoded:
What's confusing is that Starlink isn't actively advertising the Mini kit perk, and it doesn't show up on its site when signing up for a new 100Mbps or 200Mbps plan, though it still appears as part of the MAX plan. Many customers who shared the email online were surprised by the offer and assumed they weren't eligible when signing up. All this to say, it's hard to guarantee that every new Starlink Residential sign-up will get this offer.

The free Starlink Mini rental first started in early 2026, with the rebrand of the Residential Max plan, which included other perks like a free Router Mini and free professional installation. New customers were told they would get an email within a couple of weeks to claim the optional rental deal. However, some customers reported waiting months for the email, and even Starlink acknowledged the delays, citing high demand. Then the deal suddenly disappeared over the summer, only to reappear a few months later.

In a discussion of the surprise offer, one Reddit poster suggested Starlink is clearing inventory ahead of the next Starlink Mini. A new version of the Mini has been teased for months, and experts point to evidence that it will be battery-powered, making it even more portable. Earlier this summer, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk showed off a new Mini device, but didn't share details like features, pricing, or a release date. 

Starlink may be trying to ship more Mini kits before formally introducing a Starlink Mini 2 and ramping up marketing. Along with extending the Mini perk to more users, Starlink also introduced a monthly payment plan rather than a $199 upfront cost for a new Mini kit. Keeping the offer for lower-tier plan customers low-key may mean it won't be available for long, so we advise you to proceed at your own risk if you're interested in Starlink and the Mini kit incentive is a major selling point. Starlink's support page advises you to contact support to find out whether you are eligible.

item.title: When Can We Realistically Expect Amazon Leo?
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Leo has insisted that, as of summer 2026, it has enough satellites in orbit to begin internet service. However, details on what that entails are few. Will there be a beta period? Will you have to join a waitlist? How much will it cost at launch? Will the travel version, the Nano, be available at launch?  This begs the most important question: when will the average consumer be able to get their hands on Amazon Leo? Evidence points to late 2027 at the earliest.

First known as Project Kuiper, Amazon Leo promises a new rural internet solution that will leverage the company's AWS cloud capabilities and retail delivery infrastructure. It also claims it will need significantly fewer satellites than Starlink to deliver rival internet performance.

Since its announcement in 2020, the same year SpaceX officially began beta testing Starlink, Amazon Leo has faced an uphill battle to finally enter the satellite internet market as a legitimate competitor. While the work has been ongoing and the retail giant has already cemented several enterprise partnerships, delays have left the company far behind in rolling out the infrastructure needed.

item.title: Is Starlink Worth It in the City? Urban & Suburban Guide
item.content:encoded:
Starlink satellite internet has been promoted primarily as a home internet solution for rural, remote, and off-the-grid locations, but as it has gained popularity since its launch, you may wonder whether it's a viable option for home internet in more populated areas. Starlink can provide internet almost anywhere, so it will work in urban, suburban, and metropolitan areas. However, are the performance, pricing, and setup worth it compared with more traditional providers in the city?

Is Starlink Worth It in the City? Urban & Suburban Guide

Whether it's in the country or the big city, Starlink needs a clear view of the sky. However, too many Starlink dishes grouped in an area can cause congestion. | Image by Starlink

Starlink performance and network congestion

In its early days, not everyone could get Starlink, so many were added to a waitlist as the company built out its satellite constellation. Bandwidth can only be spread across so many customers. As of 2026, with more than 10,000 active satellites and more launching all the time, it's large enough to serve millions of customers and reduce network congestion. However, it's hard to determine if it's ready to be a serious competitor to traditional ISPs, including cable, DSL, and fiber. As Starlink is also entering the mobile carrier space with Starlink Mobile, its ambitions likely include general-purpose broadband.

There are more than 10,000 Starlink LEO satellites in orbit. SpaceX is consistantly launching new Starlink satellites to improve signal coverage and relieve network congestion. | Screenshot from satellitemap.space

At any given location, rural or metropolitan, Starlink's performance will vary. Anytime you begin using a Starlink dish, you're instantly competing with fellow customers around you for the satellite constellation's attention. Starlink tries to balance bandwidth between customers in several ways, mostly by expanding the constellation with layers of more advanced satellites that provide more coverage for more users. However, it also regulates congestion by adding one-time "demand surcharges" to regions with heavy usage. These congestion fees can range from $100 to $1,500. It can also limit the plans available to you, restricting access to higher-priority plans like Residential MAX. 

Network congestion exists in both rural and metro areas. It all depends on how many other Starlinks are surrounding you. In fact, because cities typically offer more options, satellite internet congestion is less likely. If there's no demand surcharge and you have access to the full range of plans, you're in the clear to use Starlink in the city.

Setup challenges in the concrete jungle

Even without network congestion, practical challenges remain when running Starlink in a metropolitan area, especially in big cities. The biggest obstacle is obtaining a clear field of view for the Starlink dish. For peak performance, aim for an unobstructed 100-degree view of the sky. Obstructions like neighboring high-rise buildings in the city or dense suburban tree lines can degrade or flat-out block the satellite signal. This can make installation tricky, especially for apartment renters who don't have access or permission to install on the roof. If that's the case, a balcony may be your best option, but if your view is of another skyscraper, you may be out of luck. 

Permanent home installation requires extra equipment and drilling. | Image by Starlink

If you own a home in the suburbs, you'll get the best performance by installing Starlink on the roof. This will require some DIY skills and extra parts, although Starlink offers professional installation (free for MAX customers and at least $199 for other plans).

To ensure Starlink will work at your location, download the Starlink app and use the obstruction tool. Use it to scan the area where you want to install the dish to confirm you have enough clearance to set it up. You don't have to be a Starlink customer to use the app.

A question of cost-effectiveness

So you can get Starlink working in your urban or suburban home without congestion or obstructions, but is it worth it? When you compare the value of satellite vs. wired connections like DSL, cable, or fiber, it's clear which is more affordable. The cost of infrastructure for satellite internet (building up the fleet through launches) accounts for its high monthly pricing. Traditional internet offered in metropolitan areas uses existing infrastructure, or investments from providers or governments, which is the case for fiber, while offering more affordable pricing.

Starlink is also unique in that it sells its equipment at a high upfront cost, with some exceptions in areas where you can rent the dish. Cable and fiber providers usually include equipment leasing in the monthly service charge.

Can Starlink compete with fiber?

While Starlink offers high speeds and low latency, is easy to obtain and install, and can be more affordable in some cases, it still falls short of the many benefits of a fiber connection. Because fiber requires new infrastructure and investment, it has been slower to adopt, but it's still growing in many metropolitan areas. A modest fiber plan can deliver at least 1 Gbps speeds with lightning-fast latency, and premium plans can offer even faster speeds. 

Another factor that separates fiber from satellite is symmetrical speeds, meaning that download and upload speeds are the same. Better upload speeds matter for transferring large amounts of data, video calling, live streaming, and overall bandwidth. Those running home businesses with servers benefit most from symmetrical speeds. Starlink is working toward 1 Gig speeds and better latency, but still lacks symmetrical speeds, with upload speeds that lag behind its top download speed. It's unclear when Starlink can rival these speeds, and as more people in a single area adopt it, congestion will always be a factor.

When does Starlink make sense in the city?

Starlink is the obvious choice for rural homes with few to no high-speed internet options, but it's hard to recommend in a big city or suburban area when there are so many more cost-effective choices. That doesn't mean Starlink doesn't have its place and can actually be a great choice in certain cases.

Even if you're surrounded by choices, they may not be appealing, especially if certain ISPs have burned you for frequent outages, poor customer service, or below-par performance. Fiber is great, but still slow to roll out and may not reach your neighborhood for a long time, if ever. Starlink is one of the few ISPs available anywhere in the U.S. If you're not a fan of your DSL, cable, or 5G options, and you're in a location that's optimal for Starlink, it's a viable option if you're willing to pay the premium.

Plus, having Starlink on hand, even when not active, is handy as a backup internet source. When your main provider goes down, Starlink can get you back online immediately. It even has a very cheap Stand-by mode that gives you minimal connection speed to stay in communication. Not to mention, you can take your Starlink with you on a Roam plan for long road trips and camping excursions.

item.title: Best Internet for Boats: Starlink Roam vs. Maritime & 5G Alternatives
item.content:encoded:
As much as we love dedicated satellite hotspots, the smartphones already in our pockets are quickly becoming capable satellite communicators on their own. If you’re boating just outside of cell range, these built-in direct-to-device features are excellent, hassle-free backups.

Apple iPhone Satellite Features Starting with the iPhone 14 lineup, Apple revolutionized mobile safety by introducing built-in satellite connectivity via the Globalstar network. If you are entirely outside of traditional cellular and Wi-Fi coverage, your iPhone can connect directly to a moving satellite (provided you have a clear view of the sky). With the recent iOS 18 update, this suite of features now includes Emergency SOS, Messages via satellite (for texting friends off the grid), and Find My via satellite. It takes a little longer to send a text this way, but as a built-in safety net, it’s an incredible value.

Starlink Direct to Cell (T-Satellite) The mobile industry is also seeing a massive shift toward carrier-provided satellite networks, spearheaded by SpaceX’s Starlink. Through a partnership with T-Mobile, Starlink recently launched T-Satellite, which uses specialized direct-to-cell satellites that act like orbiting cell towers.

If you sail out of terrestrial cell range, your phone can automatically connect to Starlink to send SMS texts, use WhatsApp, and access essential navigation and weather apps. T-Satellite is included on T-Mobile’s top-tier Experience Beyond plan, but it's also available as a $10/month add-on for other T-Mobile users—and surprisingly, even compatible AT&T and Verizon customers with an open, unlocked eSIM slot. While it won't give you the broadband speeds of a mounted Starlink Roam dish, it's a game-changer for keeping your personal phone connected on the water.

item.title: Mint Mobile MINTernet vs. T-Mobile 5G Home Internet: Which Wireless Provider Wins?
item.content:encoded:
Today, fixed wireless internet is changing the way we connect, and two compelling options run on the exact same nationwide network: T-Mobile 5G Home Internet and Mint Mobile's MINTernet.

Since T-Mobile now owns Mint Mobile, both providers leverage T-Mobile’s massive cellular infrastructure to beam internet directly to your home. But while the network is identical, how you pay for it—and how your data is prioritized—is very different. T-Mobile sticks to a traditional month-to-month postpaid model with premium perks, while Mint Mobile brings its signature bulk-prepay approach to home broadband.

Let us look at the pricing, speeds, and reliability of both options to help you decide which provider is best for your home.

item.title: SpaceX Offers Louisiana Neighbors Discounted Starlink Internet
item.content:encoded:
The people of Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, are about to get a rather large neighbor in SpaceX, so the company is offering a neighborly gift. Residents just south of Lafayette can now get a free Starlink dish and half off residential internet plans, courtesy of SpaceX. Current Starlink customers in the region will have this discount automatically applied to their accounts. This means people on the base 100Mbps plan will now pay $27.50 per month instead of $55. This applies only to home internet, not Starlink Roam plans. 

SpaceX Offers Louisiana Neighbors Discounted Starlink Internet

Residents of Vermilion Parish in the highlighted region qualify for a free Starlink kit and a discounted internet plan. SpaceX will soon break ground nearby on what it claims will be the world's largest rocket launch site. | Image by Starlink

Home of the future Spacebase

SpaceX announced that the Louisiana wetlands will be home to its planned Spacebase. The company aims to make it the future hub for its Starship craft, planning to launch it thousands of times a year. It's said to be the largest launch facility in the world when completed. The Starship will carry tons of cargo to orbit and beyond, including thousands of more Starlink satellites.

The base will take multiple years of construction and significant investment from SpaceX, so it's laying the groundwork to win over the community. It applied the same special discount to areas around Memphis, Tenn., and Southaven, Miss., earlier this Summer since it's the site of xAI's Colossus data centers. The incentive came at a time when data centers across the country are facing scrutiny from neighboring communities that criticize the space they occupy and the noise and pollution from on-site generators.

The Vermilion Parish area is easily considered rural, making it an ideal place for Starlink to build a large foothold.

How does the Starlink discount work?

The discount is automatically applied at checkout on the website when purchasing a new Starlink kit with a monthly plan. According to Starlink, the discount applies to the next bill for current customers. A support page doesn't indicate how long the promotion will be available or whether the discount is limited-time or permanent. 

Keep the promotion restrictions in mind. The discount is location-locked, so you'll be unable to simply order a free Starlink in the discount region and take it elsewhere. If it's activated at a different address, Starlink will bill you the full amount.

item.title: Starlink Is Now Paying Customers Cash to Refer a Friend
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX is now paying you to refer Starlink to family and friends through its revamped customer referral program, which lets current users earn a free service credit or $100 in cash for every friend they refer to Starlink residential service. Both the customer and the referee will get a credit for a month of standard service, 60 days after the friend activates and keeps their Starlink service. 

Customers who log into their Starlink account will immediately see the referral feature. In the Starlink app, the option appears as "Free month for you and them." Starlink offers several ways to share referral links with new buyers, including email, text messages, and QR codes. The referee needs to use the provided link to purchase their Starlink dish and service plan on the website, just as they normally would.

The referral link applies to any Starlink plan and offers credits for both Residential and Roam plans. Priority plans are excluded. The person must pay for the dish and the first two months of service using the link before using the credit. The offer won't apply to Starlink kits purchased at retail locations. Also, remember that new customers will still need to pay any regional congestion fee if they live in a high-bandwidth area.

There’s currently no limit on how many people a customer can refer. The account even keeps a tally of the referrals and credits earned, incentivizing customers to seek out as many referrals as possible. However, they warn that using the referral to make money is against the terms of service and grounds for suspension. 

The new program is currently available to customers in the U.S., Australia, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, New Zealand, Portugal, and Spain. Starlink does not specify how long the program will run, but it reserves the right to cancel the feature at any time.

item.title: How to Get Free Starlink Service After a Natural Disaster
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX and Starlink have historically been proactive in providing emergency assistance during natural disasters, often offering free internet service during and after these events. Hurricanes, earthquakes, flooding, and wildfires have prompted Starlink to activate free service when local infrastructure is damaged. Traditional ISPs often suffer outages during and after a natural disaster and can take time to resume operations. Since Starlink only needs a reliable

This response has made owning a Starlink dish worth it if you live in an area susceptible to one of these events, even if it's not your primary internet provider. Starlink has previously deployed free service to the Southern U.S. after multiple hurricanes and during the 2025 Los Angeles fires, as well as dozens of others worldwide.

Follow this page for the latest information on where Starlink is available for free in the event of a natural disaster in the U.S.

item.title: Viasat Business Satellite Internet Review
item.content:encoded:
Viasat Business Satellite Internet Review

Viasat Business Internet is a satellite internet service designed to operate in areas where cable and fiber internet aren’t available. It works best for rural businesses, remote offices, and temporary job sites that need basic connectivity. Wired internet performs much faster, but Viasat supports everyday tasks like email, web browsing, cloud portals, and point-of-sale systems when wired internet is out of reach, and 5G is too weak.

In this review:

Is Viasat the right choice for your business?

If your business is in an area where cable or fiber isn’t available, Viasat satellite internet may be one of the few ways to get online without waiting for wired infrastructure to reach your area.

The biggest tradeoff is performance. Viasat can support email, web browsing, cloud portals, and point-of-sale systems, but it’s not the best fit for teams that spend a lot of time on video calls, upload large files, or rely on cloud-heavy tools all day. If cable, fiber, or fixed wireless internet is available, it will usually offer faster speeds, lower latency, and stronger day-to-day performance.

For rural businesses, remote offices, or temporary job sites, Viasat fills a connectivity gap when stronger wired or wireless options are limited. It can also work as a backup option if your business needs another way to get online during an outage.

Viasat Business plans and pricing

Viasat Business Internet plans are built for businesses that need connectivity where cable or fiber service is unavailable. Speeds are lower than most wired options, but the plans can support basic business tasks in rural offices, remote sites, and temporary job sites.

Pricing depends on the plan, speed, data allowance, and contract length. Some plans are built for businesses that need more data for everyday use, while others may work better for lighter internet needs or backup internet. Viasat also offers unlimited plans, but that doesn’t always mean unlimited high-speed data. Speeds can slow during congestion after you use your plan’s high-speed data.

Most Viasat Business Internet plans require a contract, so it’s worth checking the full terms before signing up.

Viasat backup internet options

Viasat can also work as backup internet if your business needs another way to get online during an outage. That can be helpful for rural businesses, job sites, or locations where wired internet is limited or goes down often.

A satellite backup plan won’t be as fast or consistent as fiber or cable, but it can help keep basic work moving. It may be enough for email, web browsing, point-of-sale systems, and other simple tools until your main connection is back.

In many cases, 5G or LTE internet is a more common backup option. But if your business already uses 5G as its main connection, or if cellular coverage is not reliable at your location, satellite backup may still make sense.

Before choosing Viasat for backup internet, look at the plan terms, equipment costs, and monthly price. Backup internet still adds another cost to your business, so make sure it makes sense for how often you think you’ll need it.

Viasat Business pros and cons

Viasat Business Internet is less about getting the fastest internet and more about getting connected in places where wired providers don’t reach. That makes it useful for rural businesses, small offices, and temporary or pop-up job sites.

Before you sign up, take a close look at what the plan includes. Viasat can cover basic connectivity needs, but it is not the strongest fit for teams that rely heavily on video calls, large file uploads, or cloud-based tools throughout the day. You’ll also want to check the contract, data limits, and fees before you pick a plan, because those details make a big difference over time.

Other rural business internet options

Viasat Business Internet is a practical option when your business can’t get a strong wired connection. But if you do have other options at your address, it’s still a good idea to compare them before choosing satellite.

If it’s available at your address, cable or fiber is the most dependable connectivity type for daily workloads. Otherwise, fixed wireless (4G/5G) or a digital subscriber line (DSL) may also be viable, depending on the location.

If satellite is your best option, it’s worth comparing Viasat with Hughesnet and Starlink to see which provider makes the most sense for your speed, data, and contract needs.

Hardware and installation

Viasat Business Internet uses a satellite dish and modem to get your business online. Since the dish has to be mounted and lined up correctly, most businesses will require professional installation.

A technician will install the dish, connect the modem, and activate the service at your location. Viasat does not list one standard installation price for every business plan, and any install fee may depend on the plan, location, and setup needs. Installation is more involved than cable or fiber setup, but the technician handles dish placement, modem connection, and activation.

Satellite connectivity needs a clear line of sight to the sky, so installation may depend on your building, roof access, and where the dish can be placed.

Fees, contracts, and equipment costs

Viasat Business Internet can come with more costs than the monthly price you see upfront. Depending on the plan, your bill may also include taxes, surcharges, equipment fees, installation costs, or other charges.

Review the contract terms closely. Most Viasat business plans require either a 24- or 36-month agreement, so it’s important to understand the full term of your commitment before signing up. If you cancel early, you may be subject to an early termination fee.

Be sure to check how long your monthly rate is guaranteed. Some plans start with promotional pricing, which means your bill may go up after the promo period ends. Viasat business equipment is leased for $15 per month, and you’ll need to return it if you cancel service or you could be charged an unreturned equipment fee.

Final verdict: Is Viasat satellite internet the right choice for your business?

Viasat Business Internet is an optimal choice for businesses without access to cable or fiber. Wired internet will usually be faster, more consistent, and better for teams that use video calls, cloud software, or large file uploads every day, but it's rarely available in rural settings.

Viasat fits best where wired providers are unavailable or unreliable. For rural businesses, remote offices, or temporary job sites, it can be a useful way to get online and keep basic work moving.

Before signing up, look closely at the plan details. Contract length, data terms, equipment costs, and promotional pricing can all affect what you actually pay and how the service works over time. If you’re in a remote area and satellite is one of your only connectivity options, Viasat Business Internet can make sense. If you have cable, fiber, or another strong connection available, compare those first.

A business internet consultant can help compare rural internet providers, backup internet options, and plans based on how your business uses connectivity.

Call 833-970-5891 to get tailored solutions for your rural internet needs.

Viasat Business Internet FAQs

Does Viasat Business Internet have unlimited data?

Some Viasat Business Internet plans include unlimited data, but that doesn’t always mean unlimited high-speed data. After you use the plan’s high-speed data, your speeds may slow during times of network congestion. Review both data terms and monthly pricing before choosing a plan.

Is Viasat Business Internet good for small businesses?

Viasat Business Internet can work for small businesses that need basic internet access in areas where 5G and wired options aren’t available. It’s best for everyday tasks like email, web browsing, cloud portals, and point-of-sale systems. It may not be the best fit for businesses that rely heavily on video calls, large file uploads, or cloud-based tools all day.
